title: Ἐχθροὶ δύο
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 114 (= Perry 68). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Δύο τινὲς ἀλλήλοις ἐχθραίνοντες ἐπὶ τῆς αὐτῆς νεὼς ἔπλεον, ὧν ἅτερος μὲν ἐπὶ τῆς πρύμνης, ἅτερος δὲ ἐπὶ τῆς πρώρας ἐκάθητο.
sentences.tr: Dyo tines allēlois echthrainontes epi tēs autēs neōs epleon, hōn hateros men epi tēs prymnēs, hateros de epi tēs prōras ekathēto.
sentences.l: Two men, being at enmity with one another, were sailing on the same ship, of whom the one sat at the stern, the other at the prow.
sentences.i: Two men who hated each other were sailing on the same ship; one of them sat at the stern, the other at the prow.
sentences.n: ἐχθραίνω takes the dative of the person one hates. ἅτερος is the crasis of ὁ ἕτερος, which is why it carries a rough breathing; repeated, ὁ μέν … ὁ δέ fashion, it sets one man against the other. νεώς is the Attic genitive of ναῦς.

sentences.t: Χειμῶνος δὲ ἐπιγενομένου καὶ τῆς νεὼς μελλούσης ἤδη καταποντίζεσθαι, ὁ ἐπὶ τῆς πρύμνης τὸν κυβερνήτην ἤρετο πότερον τῶν μερῶν τοῦ πλοίου πρότερον μέλλει καταβαπτίζεσθαι.
sentences.tr: Cheimōnos de epigenomenou kai tēs neōs mellousēs ēdē katapontizesthai, ho epi tēs prymnēs ton kybernētēn ēreto poteron tōn merōn tou ploiou proteron mellei katabaptizesthai.
sentences.l: And a storm having come on and the ship being already about to be sent to the bottom, the man at the stern asked the helmsman which of the two parts of the vessel was going to be submerged first.
sentences.i: When a storm came on and the ship was already on the point of going down, the man at the stern asked the helmsman which of the two ends of the vessel would go under first.
sentences.n: Two genitive absolutes in a row (χειμῶνος ἐπιγενομένου, τῆς νεὼς μελλούσης): a noun and participle in the genitive, standing outside the sentence's own construction, setting the circumstances the main clause happens in. You will meet this constantly. πότερον is the interrogative pronoun with a partitive genitive (τῶν μερῶν), 'which of the two' — exactly two, prow and stern, which is what makes the question worth asking.

sentences.t: Τοῦ δὲ τὴν πρώραν εἰπόντος· « Ἀλλ’ ἔμοιγε οὐκ ἔστι λυπηρόν, εἶπεν, ὁ θάνατος, εἴγε ὁρᾶν μέλλω πρὸ ἐμοῦ τὸν ἐχθρὸν ἀποθνῄσκοντα. »
sentences.tr: Tou de tēn prōran eipontos· « All’ emoige ouk esti lypēron, eipen, ho thanatos, eige horan mellō pro emou ton echthron apothnēiskonta. »
sentences.l: And the helmsman having said the prow, « But to me at least death is not painful, » he said, « if indeed I am going to see my enemy dying before me. »
sentences.i: When the helmsman answered that it was the prow, he said: « Then death is no grief to me at all, if I am to see my enemy die before I do. »
sentences.n: πρὸ ἐμοῦ is temporal here, not spatial: the enemy in the bow will go under first, and the speaker, seated at the stern, will watch him drown while he still lives. The point of the fable hangs on that word. εἴγε, 'if indeed', treats the condition as granted.

sentences.t: Ὁ μῦθος δηλοῖ ὅτι πολλοὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων οὐδὲν τῆς ἑαυτῶν βλάβης φροντίζουσιν, ἐὰν τοὺς ἐχθροὺς μόνον ἴδωσι πρὸ αὐτῶν κακουμένους.
sentences.tr: Ho mythos dēloi hoti polloi tōn anthrōpōn ouden tēs heautōn blabēs phrontizousin, ean tous echthrous monon idōsi pro autōn kakoumenous.
sentences.l: The fable shows that many of men take no thought at all for their own harm, if only they see their enemies coming to grief before them.
sentences.n: φροντίζω takes the genitive of what one is concerned about; οὐδέν beside it is the adverbial accusative, 'not a bit'. κακουμένους is a supplementary participle after ἴδωσι — with verbs of perceiving, Greek says 'see them being harmed', not 'see that they are harmed'.
